title: The Pilgrim's Tale
subtitle: Seven Days with Ignatius of Loyola for the Camino Baztanes
author: CaminoPlus

spans.t: This is a small book of seven days, made to go with the Camino Baztanes. In the CaminoPlus catalogue that road runs from Bayonne to Pamplona, through France and into Spain, and the app's route notes describe it as hilly, with forest paths, and rain common. The catalogue gives no length for it, and neither does this book. Seven days is the length of the reading, not a plan of stages. If your road is longer, read a day twice. If it is shorter, keep a day for the evening after.
Why this book for this road

The book is the autobiography of Ignatius of Loyola, a soldier who became a pilgrim, and it starts where the Baztanes ends. The account tells of a young man defending the citadel of Pamplona against the French, struck by a cannon ball that broke one of his legs and badly hurt the other. Historians put the siege in 1521. The edition we use gives no year for it. Everything in the book comes out of that wound: a long time lying still, a change of mind, and then a road. The account calls him the pilgrim.

So you may finish the walk in the city where the story begins. The app's route notes say the Baztanes joins the Camino Francés at Pamplona. The edition names Bayonne once, in its last chapter, but it does not say what road Ignatius took, and this book does not claim that he walked this one.
How a day works
Each day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from the autobiography, in the exact words of a 1900 edition, spelling and all. It writes
Pampeluna
for Pamplona, and we leave it as it is. Read the passage twice, the second time aloud if you can.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Ignatius's. It starts from something on the road and lets the passage open it. It says what the passage says, where it is hard to accept, and what it might mean for an ordinary day.
For the walk.
A question and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. Both are better done on your feet than on paper.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back at the day you have lived, with two or three questions to lie down with. You need not write anything.
A short prayer.
Original and brief. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish.

spans.t: A Catholic book, and a strange one in places

The autobiography is a Catholic book, and this is a Catholic edition of 1900. It tells of visions, long fasts and scourging, written by a man who believed in all of it, and some of it is hard to read. We chose passages that a walker can follow, and where one is strange, the reflection says so. Nothing here asks you to copy the penances, and nobody should hurt themselves to read this book well. If you carry a pain you cannot shake, talk to someone you trust or to a doctor. In Spain and France, 112 is the emergency number.

People walk for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All are welcome here. You do not need to believe what Ignatius believed to recognise a man who was hurt, bored, vain, afraid, and starting again.
The shape of the seven days
The days keep to the order of the account, and they also follow a walk.

items.t: Day 1
, the soldier and his wound.
Day 2
, the long lying-still, and two kinds of thought.
Day 3
, setting out.
Day 4
, the vigil, and the road from Montserrat.
Day 5
, Manresa, and a river.
Day 6
, begging and trusting.
Day 7
, the way on.

spans.t: These are a shape, not a timetable. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk, or in a café while the soup arrives. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last of all, when the boots are off. At home it works the same way: the morning with your tea, the evening before bed.
Two words you will meet.
Albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man

Ignatius of Loyola was born in 1491 at the château of Loyola, in the north of Spain, and died on 31 July 1556. Those two dates are the ones the appendix of our edition gives, and we keep to them. He was a soldier and then a student, and in the end the founder of the Society of Jesus, whose members are called Jesuits. Catholics honour him as a saint, and the title of the edition calls him St. Ignatius. He also wrote a book called the
Spiritual Exercises
, which this book does not use.
The book

The account of his life was not written by Ignatius's own hand. In the preface of the scribe, Father Louis Gonzalez, we read that members of the Society had often asked Ignatius for the story of his life, and that he had put them off. In 1553 he agreed, and began to tell it that September. He was in very feeble health by then, and it went on in pieces, between other business, until 1555. The scribe says that his custom was to dictate while walking. He also says that he wrote down nothing he had not heard from Ignatius, and kept so close to his words that afterwards he could not always explain them.
Ignatius spoke of himself in the third person, and this edition writes
Ignatius
most of the time and
the pilgrim

now and then. The pages are not always a pure voice, either. Someone else can be heard in them, the scribe or the editor, as in the phrase "we dare not state it". That is why this book says "the account" or "the edition" where a plain "Ignatius said" would claim too much.

The edition's numbers do not always fit together. The account puts the end of his worldly years in his twenty-sixth year, and the appendix gives his age at Montserrat as thirty. We do not try to settle that.
Why it suits a pilgrim
Pilgrim

is the account's own word for him. It is a story of walking: of begging, sleeping outdoors, storms, fevers and being laughed at. Ignatius is not shown as a hero who knows the way. He is often afraid, ill, wrong or alone, and the account says so. It is also the story of a mind changing slowly, in a bed, in a church, beside a river, and a long walk gives a person that kind of time.
What is hard, and what we left out

The account has visions and penances that nobody should copy. It also has an early episode on the road, in which Ignatius nearly follows a stranger to do him harm after a quarrel about belief. The edition speaks of that stranger, and of others, in the language of 1900, which is sometimes unkind. We left those places out.

Beyond that, we took seven short passages from four of the account's eight chapters, and skipped the middle: the voyage to Jerusalem, the prisons of Alcalá and Salamanca, and the years in Paris. The account goes on to Venice and Rome, and our last day stops at the beginning of that road.
The edition and the licence
The text is
The Autobiography of St. Ignatius

, edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., printed in New York, Cincinnati and Chicago by Benziger Brothers in 1900. The title page carries church approvals dated December 1899 and a copyright notice of 1900 in the name of the printers. The edition is old enough to be in the public domain. It is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 24534, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word.

The edition names an editor, but no translator. It does not say who put the account into English, or from which language. The only translation it mentions is a Latin one, in a heading above the scribe's preface. So the passages here are credited to the edition and its editor, as the edition gives them, and no more.
We changed nothing in the passages. We kept the edition's spellings, such as
Pampeluna

, and its quotation marks. Where a passage skips a stretch, a mark like this shows it: …. We quote only the account itself, never the editor's preface, the scribe's preface or the appendix. The choice and order of the passages, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.

chapters.title: Day 1. The citadel and the wound

spans.t: What are you holding on to at the start of this walk, and what would it take to put it down?
The passage

paras.t: Up to his twenty-sixth year the heart of Ignatius was enthralled by the vanities of the world. His special delight was in the military life, and he seemed led by a strong and empty desire of gaining for himself a great name. The citadel of Pampeluna was held in siege by the French. All the other soldiers were unanimous in wishing to surrender on condition of freedom to leave, since it was impossible to hold out any longer; but Ignatius so persuaded the commander, that, against the views of all the other nobles, he decided to hold the citadel against the enemy. … Ignatius stood fighting bravely until a cannon ball of the enemy broke one of his legs and seriously injured the other. When he fell, the citadel was surrendered. When the French took possession of the town, they showed great admiration for Ignatius.

cite.t: , Chapter I (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

The first morning of a long walk is the most confident one. The pack is where you put it. Nothing has rubbed, nothing aches, and the whole road is still an idea, which is the lightest thing you will carry.

The young man in this passage was confident in just that way, and the account does not flatter him. His heart, it says, was held by the vanities of the world. He loved soldiering, and what he wanted was
a strong and empty desire of gaining for himself a great name
. Those are the words of an old man dictating near the end of his life, and an old man may judge his younger self more harshly than the younger self would have done. But he keeps the word
empty

Then the siege. The French have surrounded the citadel at Pamplona, and the other soldiers want to give it up on condition that they may leave freely, because nobody can hold out any longer. Ignatius persuades the commander to hold it. The passage gives him no plan, only the power to persuade. It does not say what that choice cost the men beside him, and we will not guess. It is the story as one man tells it, and he is the one who won the argument.
Then a cannon ball. It breaks one leg and badly hurts the other, and the citadel is surrendered as soon as he falls. A little further on, the edition says that he received
the best care from the physicians of the French army
before he was
borne on a litter to Loyola
. The man who would not yield was nursed by the people he had refused to yield to.
His recovery was slow. The bones had knit badly, so the doctors decided to break the leg again and set it properly. He let them cut him again, and gave no sign of suffering except
tightly clenching his fists

. Later, when a bone stood out below the knee and one leg was shorter than the other, he could not bear the look of it, because he meant to live at court. He asked for the bone to be cut away, though the doctors warned him that it would hurt more than everything before. He chose it. The wish for a great name had not gone anywhere. It was lying in bed with him.

Two things in all this are hard. The first is the verdict. Not every wish to be good at something, or to be known for it, is empty, and the passage should not be read as a ban on ambition. It is one man's judgement on one wish, made in hindsight. The second is the war. The account admires courage in a siege and says nothing of the dead. We read the passage for what comes after the siege, not for the siege.

The everyday version is quieter. You will not need a cannon ball. A blister, a knee, a night without sleep and a forecast of rain can do the same work. The plan for today was written by a more confident person than the one now walking, and it is easy to cling to it against all the evidence, out of the same stubbornness that held a citadel. Pace, distance, being first up, a number on a watch: everyone has their own great name to make. And nobody should do what he did with the bone. No look, and no plan, is worth choosing pain for.

There is also doubt to be honest about. The old story is tidy: the wound leads to the books, and the books to the road. Real interruptions do not always lead anywhere, and a bad knee is sometimes only a bad knee. All the passage can fairly offer is that a stop is not nothing, and that what you gripped hardest at the start may be the first thing you are glad to put down.
For the walk

items.t: What am I trying to prove on this road, and to whom? You need not answer it today. It is enough to notice that it is there, walking beside you.

At your first stop, before you look at how far is left, ask your feet, your shoulders and your hips how they are, and answer honestly. Then change one thing: loosen a strap, smooth a sock, ease the pace a little. It takes two minutes, and the rest of the day will thank you. If everything is fine, say so and walk on. The practice was the asking.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Take your boots off first, and look at your feet before you look at anything else. They have been keeping the day's true account, and they do not exaggerate.

Go back over the hours between this morning and now. There was probably a moment when the plan said one thing and the body said another. Which of them won? Sometimes the plan should win, and the hill is simply there to be climbed. Sometimes the body is right and the plan was only pride in new boots. It is hard to tell in the moment, but the day is mostly over, so you can ask the question tonight without having to act on it.

There may also have been a moment when you wanted to be seen: to arrive before someone else, to be taken for fit, or experienced, or good company, or quiet and wise. The account is blunt about its young soldier, and also gentle. It does not scold him. It only says, in one word, that what he reached for was empty. You need not be harder on yourself than that. The wish to be admired is among the oldest we have, and it walks every road.

Then look for what came the other way. In the story, the French physicians were kind to a man who had held out against them. Was anyone kind to you today for no reason you had earned? Someone who held a gate, pointed out a turning, or made room on a bench? That kindness is as much a part of the day as your pace.

Name one thing that was good, too, and let it be small. The hour when the legs warmed up and the pack stopped being something you carried and became something you wore. A hot drink. The first stretch when you stopped checking and simply walked. A first day is mostly effort, and it is easy to go to bed with only the effort in mind. If other walkers were about, you may have measured yourself against them without meaning to. Let that go with the boots.

The passage leaves one question open, and it can be asked quietly tonight. What would have happened if the soldiers had been allowed to surrender? You might ask the same of a stubbornness of your own: a quarrel, a plan, an old refusal. You need not give it up. Only look, once, at what it has cost, and who paid.

A first day tires you twice over, in the legs and in the nerves, and it is often the nerves that keep you awake. If sleep does not come, do nothing clever with the questions below. Let them lie there like a second pillow, and leave them until morning.

items.t: Where today did I push on when my body asked me to stop?
What did I want people to think of me on the road?
Who was kind to me today without being asked?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me set down what is only pride, and keep what is only courage. For the kindness I did not earn, thank you. For the feet that carried me, thank you. Let me sleep tonight, and begin again tomorrow a little lighter.
Which of your thoughts leave you lighter afterwards, and which leave you dry?
The passage

paras.t: As Ignatius had a love for fiction, when he found himself out of danger he asked for some romances to pass away the time. In that house there was no book of the kind. They gave him, instead, "The Life of Christ," by Rudolph, the Carthusian, and another book called the "Flowers of the Saints," both in Spanish. By frequent reading of these books he began to get some love for spiritual things. … This succession of thoughts occupied him for a long while, those about God alternating with those about the world. But in these thoughts there was this difference. When he thought of worldly things it gave him great pleasure, but afterward he found himself dry and sad. But when he thought of journeying to Jerusalem, and of living only on herbs, and practising austerities, he found pleasure not only while thinking of them, but also when he had ceased. This difference he did not notice or value, until one day the eyes of his soul were opened and he began to inquire the reason of the difference. He learned by experience that one train of thought left him sad, the other joyful. This was his first reasoning on spiritual matters.

cite.t: , Chapter I (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

There are days on the road when the legs finish before the day does. A fever, a wet afternoon, a rest day taken because the body insisted. You find yourself indoors with nothing to do, and the one thing still moving is your mind.

That was Ignatius's situation for a long while, with a broken leg, and the edition is plain about what he read. He wanted romances, stories of adventure, to pass the time, and the house had none. They gave him instead
The Life of Christ

, by Rudolph the Carthusian, and a book about the saints, both in Spanish. He did not choose them. They were what the house had. By reading them often, the account says, he began to get some love for spiritual things.

The account is more interested in what went on in his head. One daydream, above all the others, held him for hours at a time: what he would do in honour of a certain lady, the journey to her city, the words he would say, the exploits that would please her. The edition adds, plainly, that he never noticed how far above his reach she was. Then came the other daydream. “What if I should do what St. Francis did?” he asked himself, and then the same of St. Dominic. The two kept taking turns, and for a long while he was carried along by both.
What he noticed in the end was not what the thoughts said, but what they left behind. The worldly ones were pleasant while they lasted, and afterwards he found himself
dry and sad
. The others, about Jerusalem and a plain life, pleased him while he thought them and went on pleasing him after he stopped. The account says that it took him a while to see this, until one day
the eyes of his soul were opened
, and that he learned it by experience. Nobody told him. He found it out by lying still and paying attention to the aftertaste of his own thoughts.

It is worth saying that this was slow. The edition tells us that for a long time he did not notice or value the difference. Weeks of lying still gave him a kind of attention that few of us can find. A walker does not have the weeks, but may have something similar: hours of the same movement, until the mind slows enough to hear itself.

That is a test a walker can use with nothing else in the pack. Long days give the mind room to run, and it runs in loops: the argument replayed, the worry rehearsed, the plan polished, the old scene. Some of these leave you lighter. Some leave you flatter than you were. You do not have to stop the loops. You only have to notice how each one ends.

Two places here need a calm word. The first is the vocabulary. In the sentences just after this passage, the edition says that the two kinds of thought came from two different spirits, the spirit of God and the devil. You do not need those words to try the test. The observation stands on its own, and anyone can make it.

The second is that gladness is no guarantee. The thoughts that pleased him included living only on herbs and practising austerities. A thought can cheer you and still be unwise. A little later the account says that he knew even less of
the value of discretion

, and its pages on his year at Manresa, which we come to on Day 5, are hard reading. Nobody should take this day as a reason to fast, or to hurt themselves, because an idea felt good. If a glad thought asks something of your body, ask a friend or a doctor before you act on it.
In practice the whole of it is small. Notice. Give the aftertaste a word. That is all he did at the beginning, and the account counts it as the start of something.
For the walk

items.t: After the last hour of thinking, am I lighter or drier?

Choose one thought that keeps coming back today: a worry, a plan, a scene you keep replaying. The next time you sit down, notice what it leaves behind, and give it one word: lighter, flatter, or no change. Do not argue with the word, and do not try to fix anything. Keep a quiet tally until tonight, with marks in your head or three pebbles moved from one pocket to the other. And if the word is flatter, check the body before you blame the thought: have you eaten, and have you had water?

spans.t: At the end of the day
Supper is over, and the hour between supper and sleep begins, when thoughts run longest. It is a good hour for the tally.

Think back to the thought you chose this morning, if you chose one. How many times did it come, and how did it leave you each time? Perhaps it was always the same. Perhaps it changed with the weather, or with what you had eaten, or with whom you were walking beside. Be curious about that, and do not be hard on yourself. Nobody has only one kind of thought, and the account does not pretend that Ignatius did. His two kinds took turns for a long time before he saw the pattern.

Think, too, about what you fed your mind today. The edition says that he began to love what he read often, and in the end it changed him. What did you read, hear or watch today, and what did you keep going back to: the news, a song, a conversation, silence? You are not asked to judge it. It is only worth knowing what has been going in.

A word about the sad ones. Before you decide that a dry, flat thought is telling you something, check the body. Hunger, thirst, a skipped rest and a long climb can all make a mind go grey, and a glass of water and an early night are a better answer than any amount of examining. The account's patient lay in bed with time on his hands. You may be sitting up with cold feet.

Thoughts of people count in the tally, too. The friend you miss, the quarrel you carry. Some memories leave a person warmer, and some leave them harder. There is nothing to fix tonight. It is enough to know which is which.

And a word about the glad ones. Was there a gladness today that wanted you to do something more, to walk further than you should, to give up sleep, to take on a hardship for its own sake? Take such a gladness seriously, and put it beside what your legs and your friends would say. Joy that is real can wait for the morning, and it is often still there.
If you saw nothing today, nothing has gone wrong. The attention comes back, and so does the question. If your mind is quiet tonight, that is a good day's work too, and there is nothing to examine.

Before you sleep, pick out the lightest thing of the day, the thought or the moment that left you better than it found you, and keep it in mind for a minute. Not to prove anything. It is a small kindness to give a tired mind something light to fall asleep on, and it costs nothing. The loops will still be there in the morning, if they want you.

items.t: Which thought did I come back to most today, and how did it leave me?
Was there a gladness today that I should check against what my body and my friends would say?
What am I carrying tonight only because I am tired, and could leave until morning?

spans.t: A short prayer

May I notice what my thoughts leave behind, and be gentle with what I find. Let me not mistake tiredness for sorrow, or a bright idea for a wise one. Give me the patience of someone lying still. Let the night be quiet.
What would you settle, or set down, before you go on?
The passage

paras.t: Ignatius, starting from his father's house, set out upon his journey on horseback. … His brother desired to accompany him as far as Ogna, and during the journey was persuaded by the Saint to pass one night of watching at the shrine of Our Blessed Lady at Aruncuz. Having prayed some time at the shrine for new strength for his journey, leaving his brother at Ogna at the house of their sister, to whom he paid a short visit, he journeyed on to Navarre. Remembering that an official in the Duke's palace owed him some money, he collected it by sending in a written account to the treasurer, and distributed it among persons to whom he felt indebted. A portion of the money he devoted to the restoration of a picture of the Blessed Virgin. Then dismissing his two remaining servants, he rode forth alone from Navarre in the direction of Montserrat, a mountain town of Catalonia in the northern part of Spain.

cite.t: , Chapter II (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

The evening before a long walk is full of small errands. A key to leave with a neighbour. A message to the person who will worry. A bill to pay before it is forgotten, a plant to water, a door to check twice. None of it is the walk, and yet most people feel that they cannot really leave until it is done.

Ignatius does the same, on a larger scale. He starts from his father's house on horseback. His brother goes with him as far as a place the edition calls Ogna, and agrees, at Ignatius's urging, to spend a night of watching at a shrine on the way. There Ignatius prays
for new strength for his journey
. So the first stage of leaving is not a hurry. It is a night in a quiet place, in a brother's company, asking to be strong enough.

The edition is brisk about the partings. He leaves his brother at the house of their sister, pays her a short visit, and goes on. There is no scene. Some people leave like that, with a practical briskness that is a form of tenderness, and some with a briskness that is a way of not feeling it. The passage does not tell us which this was.

Then the accounts. He remembers that an official in the Duke's palace owes him money, and he gets it back by sending a written statement to the treasurer. He does not pretend to be above such things. Next he gives the money away, to the people to whom he felt indebted, and puts a part of it toward the restoration of a picture. The passage names no sums and no reasons beyond that one word,
indebted
. What it shows is a man leaving tidily, collecting what is his and paying what is owed, in both directions, so that nothing hangs behind him.
Last, he dismisses his two remaining servants and rides on
alone

. The passage does not say where the servants went. A servant dismissed is a life rearranged, and the edition passes over it. If today's walking is in Navarre, you are in the region that this passage crosses, though the edition does not say which roads he took.

There are things here that no walker should copy. Ignatius leaves with almost no money. A pilgrim today needs enough for a bed and a meal, a charged phone and a way to call for help, and in Spain and France the number is 112. The passage is not a lesson in packing. Nor should we slide past the sentence we have left out. The edition says that at about this time he began
the discipline
every night, which was a bodily penance. We have not quoted it, and we ask nobody to imitate it.

The idea worth taking from the passage is leaving cleanly. You cannot settle everything. But some things can be settled in a minute, and they weigh more in the pack than they do in the doing: the message you have been meaning to send, the thanks you owe, the apology you have rehearsed and not said. There is also the other direction. Some of what you are owed is not money. It is rest, a meal, a hand. Ignatius sent in his statement for what was due to him as well as paying what he owed. It is not selfish to ask for your own.

And there is a doubt to be honest about. A tidy leaving does not promise an easy road. He left with his accounts in order, and the account goes on to a hard year at Manresa, which we reach on Day 5. A clean departure is a kindness to other people and to yourself. It is not a charm.
For the walk

items.t: What is one thing I owe, or am owed, that I could settle soon? Choose something small enough for the next hour.

At your next stop, think of one person to whom you owe a thank-you, and say it in your head, slowly, in whole sentences, as if they were sitting beside you. Tonight, if it still seems right, you can send it. If it does not, you have still said it once. And if nobody comes to mind, thank whoever made or grew your last meal, in the same way.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Tonight's errands are small: boots by the door, damp things hung up, water filled for the morning. There is another errand you can run in the five minutes before sleep, and it is to look at the day as a ledger.

What did the day take from you? Some of it was effort, and some was patience, and perhaps some was money. Now what did it give? A meal, a view, a bed, a word from someone on the path. A day is a long run of small exchanges, and most of them are made without thinking. They are worth a moment's attention, if only because we usually remember what we paid, and forget what we were given.

Was there something you were given today that has not been thanked? Not a gift, perhaps, but a courtesy: a door held, an answer to a question, a bit of shade, a shared seat. A thank-you can still be said tomorrow, to the person if you meet them, and otherwise to the air.

Do not forget the one creditor who is always in the room, which is the body. It is owed water, a meal, a stretch, an early night. It sends no reminders. It sends pain instead. And if you are walking with someone, they belong in the ledger too: an hour of patience given, a share of the cost, a silence respected.

Perhaps something was owed to you today that did not arrive: a courtesy, a word of thanks, a bed you had counted on. You may feel it as a small grievance. The passage shows a man who asked for what was his, plainly, and then let the matter go. You can do the first part tonight in your head, and leave the second part to the night.

The passage also has a night of watching at a shrine, and a prayer for strength. Notice how small the request is. It is for strength for the journey, and not for the whole of life. Tonight, ask for enough for tomorrow and no more, even if you ask nobody in particular. It is a good deal easier to be strong for one day.

Tiredness has its own arithmetic, and it is a poor accountant. Things look larger at the end of a day, and old debts look heavier at night. Do not try to balance everything now. A rested person settles in ten minutes what a tired one cannot settle in an hour.

items.t: What was I given today that I have not yet thanked anyone for?
Is there something small that I owe, and could settle tomorrow?
What do I need, and no more than that, to get through tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

For what I was given today, thank you. For what I owe, give me the courage to begin paying it, and the sense to begin small. Let me ask for enough strength for tomorrow and no more. Let the people I left behind be well, and let the night be kind.
What would you put down for a day, and who else would feel it if you did?
The passage

paras.t: He begged and obtained leave of his confessor to give up his horse, and to hang up his sword and his dagger in the church, near the altar of the Blessed Virgin. … The eve of the Annunciation of Our Blessed Lady in the year 1522 was the time he chose to carry out the project he had formed. At nightfall, unobserved by any one, he approached a beggar, and taking off his own costly garments gave them to the beggar. He then put on the pilgrim's dress he had previously bought, and hastened to the church, where he threw himself on his knees before the altar of the Blessed Mother of God, and there, now kneeling, now standing, with staff in hand, he passed the entire night. … At about a league's distance from Montserrat, he was overtaken by a man who had ridden after him at a rapid pace. This man accosted him and inquired if he had given certain garments to a poor man, as the latter had declared. Ignatius answered that it was true that he had given them to a beggar. On learning that the latter had been ill-treated because he was suspected of having stolen the clothes, the eyes of Ignatius filled with tears, in pity for the poor man.

cite.t: , Chapter II (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

In the first evenings of a long walk you empty your pockets onto the bed and find that you have been carrying a different life: a work pass, a loyalty card, a key to a door you will not see for weeks. Nobody needs any of it on the road. Putting it down is quiet and a little strange, like taking off a coat you had stopped noticing.

Ignatius puts down more. In this passage he gets leave from his confessor to give up his horse and to hang up his sword and his dagger in a church, near an altar. A soldier's two tools, hung up and left. He has already bought what he needs for the road, a pilgrim's staff and a gourd to drink from, and on the night he has chosen he gives his own costly clothes to a beggar and puts on the pilgrim's dress. Then he spends the night in the church,
now kneeling, now standing
, with the staff in his hand.
The lines just before the passage show where the idea came from. He had read stories of knights who kept watch before an altar all night on the eve of being knighted, and he was, the edition says,
filled with these chivalric fancies
. So he meant to keep his vigil in the same manner, neither sitting nor lying down, and to lay aside his worldly dignities in order to take up
the arms of Christ

. There is something tender in that. The man is leaving the world of soldiers, and he does it in the costume and the manner of a soldier's story. He cannot yet imagine a new life except in the clothes of the old one. Most of us begin that way. We set out on a pilgrimage as the sort of person we already are, with the same hopes in different boots, and the road sorts the rest out slowly.

Then comes the dawn, and a hard discovery. A man rides after him, about a league from Montserrat, and asks whether he gave certain clothes to a poor man, because the poor man has said so. Ignatius says that he did. The beggar, it turns out, has been badly treated on suspicion of having stolen the clothes, and the eyes of Ignatius fill with tears,
in pity for the poor man
. The passage stops there. It does not tell us whether the beggar was freed, or what Ignatius did next.

It is a small, true thing about giving. A gift made in secret can land on someone with less power than the giver to explain it. The gesture was generous, and the cost fell on the person it was meant for. Nothing in the account says that Ignatius was wrong to give. It says only that the generosity was not the end of the matter, and that he wept.

Three things here are not for imitation. A night on your feet before a day on your feet is not advice. Sleep. The lines before the passage describe a rough sackcloth robe and a cord tied below one knee, for penance, and we have left them out. And giving away the clothes you need to a stranger is not a practice for the road, either.

The simpler question the passage leaves is what you are ready to put down. Not a sword. Perhaps a role, a title, the habit of being the competent one, the need to look as though you know where you are going. You can hang it on a hook for a day. It will probably still be there at the end, and you will know it better for having been without it. And, as the passage shows without quite saying so, you can watch who else is touched by a putting-down. Leaving a habit behind can land on a travelling companion, on someone at home, or on the person who always relied on you to decide.
For the walk

items.t: What would I put down for a day, and who would feel it if I did? Let the answer be small and true: a habit, not a possession.

At the next gate, stile or view, stand still for one full minute, with your pack on and your phone in your pocket. Do not sit. That minute is the whole vigil. When it is over, walk on at the pace you came with, and see whether anything in you has moved. If a minute feels very long, that is worth knowing too.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Tonight, unlike the man in the passage, you should lie down. Vigils belong to people who have slept enough, and the whole of tonight's work is a bed.

Before you do, think about what you set down today, even for an hour. It need not have been grand. You may have put the phone away. You may have let somebody else choose the place to eat, or walked behind instead of in front, or said nothing when you had a correction ready. Small things of that size are the true material of the day. If you set nothing down, notice that too, with interest and without blame.

Then think about the other half of the passage. Did anything you did today, meant kindly, land differently on someone else? A suggestion that sounded like a criticism. A favour that put someone in your debt. A cheerful word at a bad moment. We cannot always know, and the account does not claim that Ignatius could have known. But it is worth the minute to look, because good intentions are poor at noticing their own effects. If you find something, the answer is rarely a speech. A short, plain word tomorrow, or a changed habit, is usually enough.

The tears are worth a thought as well. The passage ends on pity, which is neither a plan nor a principle. Was there someone today for whom you felt that plain, unprofessional pity: a stranger limping, a walker who looked lost, an animal by the road? What did you do with the feeling? There is no right answer. Sometimes the most we can do is to feel it, and let it make us a little gentler with the next person.

There is one more person in the passage, and he has no name and no voice. Who on today's road had neither? Whoever served your breakfast, cleaned the room, stood behind the counter or opened the gate. You need not do anything grand. A name asked, and a thank-you given with a look in the eyes, is enough.

And think about the costume. What old story about yourself did you walk in today: the capable one, the quiet one, the funny one, the one who never needs anything? We all have a favourite suit, and the first days of a walk are when it fits least. Perhaps there was a moment today when it pinched. You do not have to take it off yet.
If you did hang something up today, look in the morning to see whether you want it back. Either answer is information.
Be as tired as you are tonight. Nothing about the road requires you to lie awake trying to improve. The day has already done what it can.

items.t: What did I put down today, even for an hour?
Did anything I did today, meant kindly, land differently on someone else?
What old story about myself did I walk in today?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me put down what I can, and see who is standing near when I do. Where my kindness has landed badly, let me notice it and not look away. Tonight let me lie down like someone with nothing left to guard. Let morning find me rested.
What do you see when you stop, and what do you owe the body that carried you here?
The passage

paras.t: One day he went to the Church of St. Paul, situated about a mile from Manresa. Near the road is a stream, on the bank of which he sat, and gazed at the deep waters flowing by. While seated there, the eyes of his soul were opened. He did not have any special vision, but his mind was enlightened on many subjects, spiritual and intellectual. So clear was this knowledge that from that day everything appeared to him in a new light. Such was the abundance of this light in his mind that all the divine helps received, and all the knowledge acquired up to his sixty-second year, were not equal to it. From that day he seemed to be quite another man, and possessed of a new intellect.

cite.t: , Chapter III (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

Somewhere on most roads the path runs beside water, and you stop without having decided to. The app's route notes for the Baztanes mention rivers and beech forests, and a stream, a bridge or a low wall will do. You sit. You are not doing anything. For a few minutes the road's usual arithmetic of distance, time and what comes next goes quiet.
That is more or less what the passage describes. Ignatius goes to a church about a mile from Manresa, and on the way he sits on the bank of a stream and watches the deep water go by. Then
the eyes of his soul were opened

. The account is careful about what did and did not happen. He had no special vision, it says. His mind was lit up on many subjects, spiritual and intellectual, and from that day everything looked new. It goes further, and this is an old man's claim: that everything he had been given and had learned in all the years up to his sixty-second year was not equal to what he was given that day. It says that he seemed
quite another man

Look at where it happens. The Manresa of the account is not a far-off retreat. He lives in a hospital and in a monastery cell, he begs his food from day to day, and he goes to Mass every day. The river is a short walk from all that. His clearing was not a far country. It was an ordinary place near an ordinary life, which is some comfort to anyone who cannot get away.
What it does not say is what he understood. The edition keeps that to itself.

It is easy to read the passage as a prize. The pages before it do not read like one. At Manresa, before the river, the account describes months of torment. He was tormented by the fear that he had not confessed everything, however many times he confessed. He prayed for hours, scourged himself, and once went a week without food or drink, until his confessor told him to eat. At the worst he cried out,
I find no remedy among men
, and was tempted several times to throw himself from the window of his cell, and he answered the temptation with a prayer.
If you carry thoughts like that, please do not carry them alone. Tell someone you trust, or a doctor, today. In Spain and France, 112 is the emergency number.

The river did not repay those months. It came afterwards, sideways, in a place he had not chosen, while he was doing nothing. Some of the changes the account names are more practical than any light. He decided that he had given enough of his time to prayer, and chose
to give sufficient time to sleep

. After a time he gave up his harshest penances and trimmed his nails and hair. So one of the things a man does after the worst of it is to start looking after his body. It is not the smallest lesson at Manresa, and a walker can borrow it without any theology.

We should be honest about the size of the claim. A man seems to himself to become another man by a stream, and the edition tells it as fact, in the voice of a story told many years afterwards. We quote it because its shape is familiar. It often seems that the answer, when one comes, arrives sideways, after the effort, in a place you did not pick. It is not a promise about your river.

For an ordinary day it comes down to a stop. You do not need a stream, and you do not need an insight. Ten minutes with nothing to produce is enough. Nothing may happen, and that is not a failure. The only thing owed to a stop is that you let it be a stop, and do not turn it into a task. Ignatius found his clearing when he sat down. It came after, and not instead of, learning to take care of himself.
For the walk

items.t: What do I see, if I look at one thing for a long time?

At the next piece of water, a stream, a fountain, a ford, stop for ten minutes. Sit if you can. Put the phone away, watch the water or the light on it, and let your mind do what it likes. Do not hunt for an insight. If the path offers no water, any slow thing will do: a cloud, or a tree moving in the wind. If someone is walking with you, they can sit beside you and say nothing, and that is a generous thing to do for each other. Afterwards, drink something, and eat if you can, before you go on.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If today was a day for stopping, the evening may bring a small guilt: kilometres you did not walk, a schedule that slipped. Set it against what you saw. A stop is a kind of arrival, and it is hard to measure on the same scale as distance.

Try to name one thing you noticed when you stopped, and let it be a real thing and not a lesson. The sound of the water. A colour in the stones. How the light moved when a cloud went over. It need not mean anything. It is enough that you saw it, and that nobody else saw it quite that way.

One practical change the account names after the dark months was to give more time to sleep. So this is a good evening for the small acts of care that no one ever notices. Look at your feet. Drink a glass of water. Stretch the places that complained today. Pack for the morning now, so that the morning is easier. Set the alarm a little later than your first instinct. None of that is glamorous, and all of it is what a long walk is made of.

A river goes on flowing whether or not you watch it. That can be taken as a mercy. The world does not need your attention in order to continue, so you can give it freely. If you notice that you are more tired than usual tonight, it may be that sort of tiredness, which comes from having been still and a little exposed for a while, and not from the kilometres.

If you saw something today, say it aloud to someone at the table, in a single sentence. A thing seen is a little more real once it has been said. And if rain came, as the route notes say it often does, it counts as water too. A wet hour with the hood up is also a way of watching the world go by.

If you sat by the water and nothing came, nothing has gone wrong. Insight is not owed to anyone, and it is not a measure of the day. A day on which you drank, ate, rested and looked at a stream has done a good deal.

And a quiet word, in case tonight is one of the dark ones. The account is honest that Ignatius had such nights, and that he went looking for someone to help him, with mixed results. If tonight is heavy, tell someone you trust, or speak to a doctor tomorrow, and if you are in danger now, call 112. A hard hour does not mean the road was a mistake.

items.t: Where did I stop today, even briefly, and what did I notice?
What did I do for my body today that had nothing to do with getting further?
Whom could I tell, if a dark hour came?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the places where the road stopped me, thank you. For water, and light on water, and the long minutes beside it, thank you. Let me care for this body as for a friend. If a dark hour comes, let me not keep it to myself. Let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 6. Bread, and the asking for it

spans.t: What do you need today, and who could you ask?
The passage

paras.t: Many offered to accompany him, but he refused, as he wished to go alone. He expected to derive great advantage from placing his whole trust in God alone. … If he took a companion, when hungry he would look to his companion for food; if exhausted, he would call on his companion for help; and so he would confide in his companion, and have some affection for him: whereas he wished to place all this confidence, hope, and affection in God alone. … When he thought of procuring bread, he was much troubled with scruples. "Is this your hope and faith in God, who, you were sure, would not fail you?" The force and violence of the temptation were such that he was greatly distressed. Good reasons on both sides presented themselves. Finally, in his perplexity, he determined to leave the matter to his confessor. He told him first of his great desire to go to Jerusalem, and to do everything for the greater glory of God. Then he gave the reasons for not taking provisions for the voyage. His confessor decided that he ought to beg what was necessary and take it with him. He went to a lady of rank to ask for what he needed.

cite.t: , Chapter III (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

At some point every day on the road the question of food arrives. A shop is shut when you reach it, or the café you counted on has no kitchen, and you open the bag to find half a loaf. The app's route notes call the Baztanes a small route and advise you to plan your stops, and food is a good thing to plan. This passage is about a man and his bread.

Ignatius is setting out for Barcelona, to take ship for Jerusalem, and many people offer to go with him. He refuses them all. The reason he gives is close to bookkeeping. If he took a companion, then when he was hungry he would look to him for food, when he was exhausted he would call on him for help, and he would come to rely on him and grow fond of him. He wanted to put all that trust, hope and affection in God alone. The edition adds, so that we do not take it for a figure of speech, that his words
were not a mere expression of the lips

Then a practical hitch. The captain of a ship will take him without a fare, on one condition: that he brings enough sailors' bread to live on. Ignatius would have refused even that, and the thought of bread plunges him into doubt. A voice in his head says,
Is this your hope and faith in God

, and goes on to remind him that he had been sure God would not fail him. Good reasons seem to stand on both sides, and he is, the edition says, greatly distressed. So he does something that the man of the first paragraph would not have predicted. He asks someone else. He puts the matter to his confessor, who decides that he should beg what he needs and take it with him. And he goes to a lady of rank to ask.

The man who would not lean on a companion is told, within a page, to go and ask for bread. His first idea of trust was to need nothing from anyone. The second, which his confessor gave him, was closer to the truth: to ask, to take what is given, and to go on. It is worth noticing who changed his mind. It was not a vision or a theory. It was one person, who listened, and said something practical.

And the edition shows him still working out where the line falls. Before he boards, he leaves five or six coins, which had been given to him as alms, on a bench on the wharf. Bread, yes. Coins, no. Nobody could call it a system, and he does not claim that it is.

There are three honest cautions. The first is that refusing a companion was one man's rule for one stage of his life, and the account does not hold it up as a law. Later in the same book Ignatius has many companions, among them the nine friends who meet at Venice. On the Camino most people walk beside others, and many are glad of it. The second is that trust is not the same as having nothing. A walker who carries water and plans a lunch is not failing at faith. His confessor said as much, in effect, when he told him to take bread. The third is that the voice that asked
Is this your hope and faith in God

belongs to what the account calls scruples, an anxious, accusing voice of the kind that tormented him at Manresa. If you hear a voice like it, you are allowed to put the question to someone else, as he did.

Nothing heroic is needed. Name one thing you need today, and ask someone for it. Water at a café counter, a pointer at a fork in the path, a pinch of salt, the time of the last bus. Say thank you, and take it. Asking is one of the harder small things on a long walk, and it often costs less than we feared.
For the walk

items.t: What do I need today, and who could I ask?

Ask one person for one small thing: a refill of water, directions you half know already, the time of the next shop. Look at them as you ask, and say thank you in full when you are given it. Notice how asking feels in the body just before the words, and how it feels just after. If asking comes easily to you, practise the other half instead: say yes to the next thing that is offered, even if you would have managed without it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Whoever is cooking tonight, or passing the bread, or pouring water into someone else's glass, is doing what the passage is about without giving it a thought. Meals are where help changes hands without being called help.

Look back over the day for the places where you asked, and the places where you did not. There may have been a moment when you wanted something, directions, a plaster, a seat, and decided it was easier to go without than to ask. Easier for whom? Sometimes the reason is independence, which is a real good. Sometimes it is only a dislike of owing. The two feel alike from the inside. The account shows a man who refused every companion on principle, and who was turned round by one short conversation. He was not weaker afterwards.

Was there also a moment when someone offered, and you waved it away? A hand with a strap, a share of food, a lift for the last stretch. Perhaps you were right to. Perhaps you will wish tomorrow that you had said yes.

And a question the other way round: whom did you trust today? A stranger's directions, a line on a map, the forecast, a word that the next village has a shop. Most of a day's walking runs on a trust so ordinary that we do not call it that. It was mostly honoured, or you would not be sitting here.

If you walked alone today, the passage may sound different tonight from the way it sounded this morning. Being alone can be a great gift and it can be heavy, and often it is both within the same hour. You do not have to decide which it was. But you might tell someone one thing about your day, at the table or in a message. It is a small way of not being entirely on your own, and it costs only a sentence.

If asking comes easily to you, turn the question round. Did you let anyone help you today, or did you do the helping and keep your hands clear of owing? Giving can be a way of staying in charge, and it is worth knowing if that was your way today.

Before you sleep, think of tomorrow's bread: a roll saved from supper, the stops you mean to make. Looking ahead is not a failure of faith, and the person who sold or cooked your food has already helped you more than you may have noticed.
Asking is harder when you are tired, and so is accepting. If you could do neither today, forgive it, and try again after breakfast, when most things are easier to ask for.

items.t: Where did I ask for help today, and where did I decide not to?
Did I turn down something that was offered, and why?
Whom did I trust today without noticing?

spans.t: A short prayer

For every hand that gave me something today, thank you. Let me ask for what I need without shame, and take what is given without hurry. Let me be easy to help and glad to help. Keep those who walk alone tonight, and keep those who walk beside me.
What is the next step, and not the whole road?
The passage

paras.t: Although at first he enjoyed good health, he afterward fell seriously ill. For this reason, after his recovery, he determined to depart in order to accomplish the business which he had undertaken for his companions. He resolved to set out on foot and without money. His brother was grieved at this, and looked on it as a disgrace to himself. Ignatius concluded to yield this point, and at last, toward evening, he consented to be carried to the boundary of the province in company with his brother and relatives. But as soon as he had left the province, he dismounted and without receiving any sustenance for the journey he set out for Pampeluna and thence to Almazonus, the birthplace of Father Laynez. Then he traveled on to Siguensa and to Toledo, and afterward from Toledo to Valencia. In all these cities, the birthplaces of his companions, he would receive nothing from their parents and relations, although they offered him a great many things, and begged him to accept them.

cite.t: , Chapter VIII (edited by J. F. X. O'Conor, S.J., 1900)

spans.t: Reflection

The end of a walk is seldom the place where the road stops. You reach the town you were walking toward, and there is a square, a church, a café, a street that carries on out of the other side. The legs have not yet been told. The Baztanes ends in Pamplona, and the app's route notes say that it joins the Camino Francés there, so for anyone who wants it, the road does go on.

In this passage Ignatius leaves home a second time, and not for himself. After an illness and a recovery he decides to go and do business that he has undertaken for his companions, the friends he made as a student in Paris, in pages of the account we have not used. He means to go on foot and without money. His brother is grieved, and takes it for a disgrace to himself. Ignatius, the edition says, yields on that one point. He lets himself be taken to the boundary of the province, toward evening, with his brother and his relatives. And as soon as he has crossed it, he gets down, and goes on without any food for the journey.

So the stubborn man is also, here, a man who bends: a little, for a brother's sake, and not further. It is a small compromise, one evening's ride. The edition does not tell us what either of them felt at the boundary. The brother's grief stays in the account, and the account does not claim that it was set right. Some departures cost someone something, and a good purpose does not undo the cost.
Pamplona is only a name in the passage. He
set out for Pampeluna

, and from there to a town the edition spells Almazonus, then to Siguensa and Toledo and Valencia. Nothing is said about what it was like for a man to walk toward the place where a cannon ball had broken his leg. The passage says only that he went on. If you arrive there at the end of the Baztanes, you may find that the place means something to you, or nothing, and both are allowed. What the passage gives you is an example of a way on that does not wait for a feeling.

In every one of those cities, the edition adds, he would receive nothing from the parents and relatives of his companions, though they offered him a great deal and begged him to accept it. On Day 6 we met the same man learning to ask for bread. Here he refuses what kind people press on him. The two do not obviously fit. It may have been strength, or stubbornness, or both, and it may have cost some generous people the pleasure of giving. If someone begs you to accept something, you are allowed to say yes.
Nor does the account make the road dignified. A little further on, it has him crawling on hands and feet along a narrow path above a river, in fear, for a long time. The account calls it
the greatest of all the bodily labors that he ever experienced
. Then, entering Bologna, he falls from a little bridge into mud, to the amusement of a crowd, and begs through the whole city without receiving
so much as a farthing
. He rests there, because he is ill, and then goes on toward Venice. That is what the way on looks like in the book: fear, mud, laughter, nothing in the hand, a rest, and then the next town.

For today, the lesson is not to wait. You do not need to know what the whole road means before you walk the next stretch. You need only the stretch, and some patience with a body that has had enough. If your road ends today, there is still the walk to the station, or home, and that is a way on too.
For the walk

items.t: What is the next step, and not the whole road? You need only answer for the next hour.

Walk the last stretch of today, the last few hundred paces or the last kilometre, at half your usual speed. Name silently three things you pass as you go: a gate, a wall, a piece of sky. When you stop, stay on your feet for one breath more, and thank your legs, in whatever words you like. A way on need not be far. It can be the next bend.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If you have walked as you read, tonight's tiredness has a week in it. It is different from the tiredness of a single day. It sits deeper, and it can make the ordinary things, a stairway, a fork, a menu, feel enormous. Take them slowly.

If you have come to the end of the Baztanes today, you might sit for a while somewhere in the city before you do anything else. A bench, a step, a quiet church if one is open. You need not feel anything in particular. Arrival often turns up late, after the shower, in the middle of an ordinary supper.

Look back at the day through the passage. Where did you go on without waiting to feel ready? And where did you bend, a little, for someone's sake, and was that the right place to bend? A point worth yielding is often small, and a point worth holding is often the one that is quietly yours. It is not always easy to tell them apart in the moment, and a day's end is a kind way to look.

Did anything happen today that made you look foolish? A wrong turning, a stumble, a coffee on your sleeve. Perhaps people laughed, or only noticed. The account tells of Ignatius in the mud at Bologna plainly, and makes no lesson of it. Some of our foolish moments are better left plain. With a little time, they may become the parts of the story we like best.
If today was hard, the account has some company for you. The way on is allowed to be ugly. It does not have to be graceful, or well timed, or admired by anyone who sees it.

The road also runs through other people's villages, fields and kitchens. Before you go on, you might thank, in your head or in person, whoever gave you water, a bed or a direction. A village is a home, and you have been a guest in it.

If someone is waiting to hear how it went, give them one true sentence tonight, and keep the long story for another day. The long story takes weeks to find its shape, and a tired person tells it badly. The legs have earned the evening, and so have you.

Before you sleep, decide only the first step of tomorrow, the one that gets you out of the door. Not the whole plan. If your walk is not over, nothing has to be settled tonight. And if one of these seven questions helped you, you could keep it, one a night, long after the days are done.

items.t: Where today did I go on without waiting to feel ready?
What small point did I yield today, and was that the right one?
What do I want to carry with me from these seven days?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the road behind me, thank you, and for the road that goes on. Let me walk the next stretch without waiting to feel ready. Let me bend where love asks it, and hold where I must. Let me be able to laugh at the mud. Rest my feet, and keep the people I love.

You have come to the end of the seven days. Perhaps you read them on seven days of walking, or over a quiet week at home, or all at once on a train. Any of those is fine. The book has no certificate to give you. It was made to keep a little company on a road, and a road has no use for a book once it is over, except to be remembered kindly.
So the only question left is what to keep. Not everything. Three small things will do, one for the head, one for the hands and one for the feet.

items.t: For the head: a test.

After a thought, a conversation or an hour of music, ask what it leaves behind. Lighter, or drier? It is the plainest thing in the book, and Ignatius found it by lying in a bed with nothing else to do. It is as useful on a train as on a path.
For the hands: one small settling.
Pay what you owe, or ask for what you need. A thank-you sent, a bill closed, a glass of water requested. A day with one of these in it is a tidier day.
For the feet: a stop, and a next step.
Ten minutes beside something that moves, with nothing to produce. And, when the road is too long to think about, only the next stretch.

spans.t: If you keep all three for a month, you will have kept a good deal from a small book.
How to go on
Come back whenever you like. The days are short, and a day that said little the first time may say more the fifth. The evenings can be read alone.

You might also read Ignatius himself. The account is in the public domain, in the edition we used, at Project Gutenberg, ebook number 24534. It runs to about eighteen thousand words, a few evenings' reading, and it tells much that we left out: the voyage to Jerusalem, the prisons, the years in Paris, the first friends, the road to Rome. Some of it is strange, and some of it will not suit you. That is allowed. A book of this kind is not a test, and some passages will have asked for more than you could give, or less than you hoped for. Leave those, and take what helped.
A last word
The account stops where it stops, in Rome, with work still going on, and with a short, plain line that hands the rest to someone else:
Master Natalis can tell the rest
. It is an odd way to close the story of a life, and a good one. The pilgrim does not announce an arrival. Others will carry on the telling.

You may or may not have reached Pamplona. Either way, the road goes on from where you are. The man who once wanted a great name tells his story, in these pages, with a great deal of being helped in it: by French physicians, by a confessor with practical advice, by a lady of rank, by a brother who rode with him to the boundary. It may be that the helped part deserves the last word.
Walk again. Next year, if you can. Or tomorrow, round the block, with your phone left behind and your hands open.
Buen Camino.
